title: Is the Economy Booming, or Just Growing?

sentences.text: The American economy grew in both quarters of 2026 we have numbers for, and yet by September the average hourly paycheck bought less than it had a year before.

assertions.text: Real GDP increased in the first and second quarters of 2026.
qualifications: s08 says this growth is about the usual pace, not a boom.

assertions.text: Real average hourly earnings for all employees decreased from September 2025 to September 2026.

sentences.text: So is this a boom, or are workers going backwards?
Which side is right depends on which number you look at.
sentences.note: Framing only; the numbers each side uses are attributed in s04-s05 and checked in the investigation.

sentences.text: Donald Trump has put one side plainly: "The economy is the greatest economy we've ever had by far."

assertions.text: Trump said the economy is the greatest economy the US has ever had.

quote.text: The economy is the greatest economy we've ever had by far.
quote.speaker: Trump

sentences.note: Trump speaking in the tape CNN rolled; the source title names him.

sentences.text: The other side points at the paycheck, and CBS News put it bluntly: inflation "is really just eating up all of the wage growth that Trump has talked about and then some".

assertions.text: A CBS News report said inflation is eating up all of the wage growth and then some.

quote.text: is really just eating up all of the wage growth that Trump has talked about and then some
quote.speaker: CBS News

sentences.text: Start with the boom: how fast is the economy actually growing?
Real GDP, the value of everything the country produces after stripping out price rises, grew at an annual rate of 2.5 percent in the first quarter of 2026 and 2.2 percent in the second.

assertions.text: BEA's third estimate: real GDP increased at an annual rate of 2.5% in the first quarter of 2026 (revised) and 2.2% in the second quarter.
qualifications: s08 says this is roughly trend growth, a solid expansion rather than a boom.

sentences.text: That is solid growth, but Federal Reserve officials put the economy's long-run pace at 2.0 percent a year, so this runs only a little above normal, not the surge the word boom suggests.

assertions.text: In the September 2026 Summary of Economic Projections, the median FOMC participant put longer-run real GDP growth at 2.0%.
qualifications: The sentence attributes the benchmark to Fed officials: it is their projection, not a measurement.

assertions.text: Real GDP growth of 2.5% and 2.2% in the first half of 2026 ran only slightly above the economy's longer-run trend pace: an expansion rather than a boom.
qualifications: This sentence is the qualification: a little above the long-run pace, not a boom.

sentences.note: The 2.0 is the longer-run median for 'Change in real GDP' in the FOMC SEP table (L17); s07's 2.5 and 2.2 are compared against it.

sentences.text: What about jobs?
The unemployment rate was 4.2 percent in September, and it has stayed between 4.1 and 4.3 percent since March.

assertions.text: The unemployment rate was 4.2% in September 2026 and has remained between 4.1% and 4.3% since March.
qualifications: s12 gives the weak payroll growth; s13 says the report does not define full employment.

sentences.text: At its September press conference, the Federal Reserve's chair said "the unemployment rate is basically running consistent with full employment".

assertions.text: The Federal Reserve chair said the unemployment rate is running consistent with full employment.

quote.text: the unemployment rate is basically running consistent with full employment
quote.speaker: Federal Reserve

sentences.note: FOMC press conference, September 16, 2026 (Federal Reserve channel); the context names 'chairman warsh'.

sentences.text: But payrolls barely moved: employers added just 29,000 jobs in September.

assertions.text: Nonfarm payroll employment changed little in September 2026 (+29,000).
qualifications: This sentence is the qualification: payrolls changed little.

sentences.note: The +29,000 is in the verdict note on this cite (the release's payroll line).

sentences.text: And the jobs report itself never defines full employment, so calling this full employment is a judgement, not a measurement.

assertions.text: The September 2026 Employment Situation release does not define full employment.
qualifications: This sentence is the qualification: full employment is not defined by the release.

sentences.text: Now the paycheck, the number most people actually feel.
In the year to January 2026, pay beat prices, and average hourly earnings after inflation were up 1.2 percent.

assertions.text: Real average hourly earnings (AHE deflated by CPI-U) rose 1.2% over the year to January 2026, as nominal pay outpaced CPI.
qualifications: s19 says these are averages across all employees.

sentences.text: Then prices jumped in the spring, and from April on, real hourly pay was lower than a year earlier in every month.

assertions.text: Real average hourly earnings were below their year-earlier level in every month from April to September 2026, while CPI ran 3.3% to 4.2%.

sentences.text: By September, pay was up 3.0 percent on the year and prices 3.7 percent, leaving real hourly earnings 0.7 percent lower.

assertions.text: Over the year to September 2026, nominal average hourly earnings rose 3.0% and CPI rose 3.7%.
From September 2025 to September 2026, real average hourly earnings for all employees decreased 0.7%, seasonally adjusted.

sentences.text: Trump's boast that wages are "rising much faster than inflation" matched the year to January; it does not match the year to September.

assertions.text: Trump said that wages are rising much faster than inflation.
assertions.speaker: Trump

assertions.text: Real average hourly earnings rose over the year to January 2026, as nominal pay outpaced CPI.
qualifications: s19 says these are averages across all employees.

assertions.text: Real average hourly earnings for all employees fell over the year to September 2026.
qualifications: s19 says the figures are averages for all employees, not the median worker.

sentences.note: Credits the boast for the year to January (s15) instead of testing it only on a later year; names Trump, the speaker in the KOMO address title.

sentences.text: One limit: these are averages across all employees, so they cannot tell you how the worker in the middle of the pay scale did.

assertions.text: The BLS real earnings figures are average hourly earnings for all employees, not a median.
qualifications: This sentence is the qualification: averages, not the median worker.

sentences.text: So is the economy booming? By these measures, no: it is growing a little faster than the Fed's long-run pace, with unemployment right at the level Fed officials expect it to settle at, but slow hiring.

assertions.text: Real GDP growth in the first half of 2026 ran only slightly above the FOMC's longer-run growth median: an expansion rather than a boom.
qualifications: The sentence itself says a little faster than the long-run pace, not a boom, and names the benchmark as the Fed's.

assertions.text: The September 2026 unemployment rate was at the FOMC participants' median longer-run unemployment rate, while payroll growth was weak.
qualifications: The sentence attributes the benchmark to Fed officials (a projection, not a measurement; s13 already says full employment is a judgement) and pairs it with slow hiring.

sentences.note: September unemployment 4.2% (BLS) equals the SEP longer-run unemployment median 4.2 (L21); no figure is read again here.

sentences.text: Growth and shrinking real pay are not a contradiction: in 2026 they ran side by side, because output, jobs and what a paycheck buys are different measurements.

assertions.text: In 2026 real GDP grew and unemployment stayed low while real hourly earnings fell, so growth and falling purchasing power coexisted; the employment side was steady rather than strong.
qualifications: s20 says hiring was slow, so the jobs side was steady rather than strong; the sentence says growth, not strong employment.

sentences.text: So the next time someone tells you the economy is booming, or that it is broken, ask one question: which number?
